app.description: Learn PySpark by aggregating synthetic sales records: totals, averages, ranks and running values by period, product and store, saved as Parquet.
app.epilog: Start here: 'sales-agg doctor' to check your setup, then 'sales-agg tour' for the whole walkthrough.
help.lang: Screen language: en or ko (default: SALES_AGG_LANG, then your system locale)
help.workdir: Folder for .spark-tmp, data/ and output/ (default: SALES_AGG_WORKDIR or the current folder)
help.seed: Random seed; the same seed always gives the same data (default: {default})
help.ui: Keep the Spark web UI at http://localhost:4040 open until you press Enter
help.rows: Number of sales records to generate (default: {default})
help.repeat: Timed runs per size; the median is reported (default: {default})
help.cmd.doctor: Check that Java 17+ is installed and the temp folder is writable
help.cmd.generate: Step 1: generate synthetic sales records and save them as CSV
help.cmd.explore: Step 2: read the CSV, build columns, see lazy evaluation
help.cmd.aggregate: Step 3: sum, average and distinct count by store, month and category; pivot table
help.cmd.window: Step 4: rank, month-over-month change, running total, 7-day moving average
help.cmd.explain: Step 5: read the execution plan and count shuffles
help.cmd.save: Step 6: save partitioned Parquet and read one month back
help.cmd.bench: Time the pipeline for growing row counts and write output/bench.csv
help.cmd.tour: Run all six steps in order (the recommended start)

doctor.install_linux: Install it with: sudo apt install openjdk-21-jdk   (or your package manager's OpenJDK {minimum}+)

error.gateway: Spark could not start its Java process (JAVA_GATEWAY_EXITED). Run 'sales-agg doctor': the usual causes are a missing or too old Java (need 17+), a wrong JAVA_HOME, or a temp folder that cannot be written.
step.what.generate: Create fake sales records inside Spark and save them as CSV files (no download needed).
step.what.explore: Read the CSV with a declared schema and build new columns. Spark only plans the work until an action runs.
step.what.aggregate: groupBy + agg: one summary row per store and month, like an Excel pivot table.
step.what.window: Window functions look at neighbouring rows without collapsing them: rank, last month, running total, moving average.
step.what.explain: Ask Spark how it will compute an aggregation and find the shuffles (Exchange lines).
step.what.save: Write Parquet with one folder per month, then read just one month back.
generate.done: Generated {requested} requested rows (seed {seed}); {actual} remain after closing store S5 on Mondays -> {path}
generate.reused: Reusing existing data for {requested} rows (seed {seed}): {actual} rows in {path}
i.generate: {closed} rows are missing on purpose: store S5 is closed on Mondays in this fake data. That is what makes the moving-average trap visible later. All patterns here come from the generator, not from real shops.
explore.lazy: Building the plan (filter + select + new column) took {plan_s}s. The count() action then took {act_s}s and counted {n} rows.
explore.sample: Five largest order lines with qty >= 3, one per store and product (amount = qty * unit_price):
explore.pandas: The same idea in pandas, for comparison:
i.lazy: Building the plan took {plan_s}s because nothing was computed yet (lazy evaluation). The real work ({act_s}s) started only when count() ran. pandas would have computed every line immediately.
aggregate.t_monthly: Store x month: sum, average ticket, distinct products (first 6 rows):
aggregate.t_pivot: Pivot: sales by store (rows) and month (columns m1..m12):
i.stores: Store {top} sold the most ({top_total}, {share}% of all sales) and {low} the least ({low_total}). The generator gave stores different size weights, so this is expected.
i.stores_single: There is only one store ({store}, {total} in total), so there is nothing to compare between stores.
i.season_single: There is only one month (month {month}, {total} in total), so there is no seasonal pattern to compare.
i.season: Month {best} is the strongest ({best_total}) and month {worst} the weakest ({worst_total}). The generator plants year-end growth and a weak February, and the aggregation finds it.
window.t_rank: Store {store}: monthly rank (1 = best store), change vs last month, running total
window.t_ma: Days where the 7-row and 7-day moving averages differ, store {store} (first 6):
i.mom: Biggest month-over-month jump: store {store}, month {month}, grew {pct}% over the month before (seasonal demand planted in the generator).
i.cum: After month {months}, store {store} has the highest running total ({cum}); it was the monthly #1 in {wins} of {months} months.
i.rows_range: rowsBetween(-6, 0) means the last 7 rows, rangeBetween(-6, 0) the last 7 days. They give different numbers once a store has days without sales (days that differ: {stores}), because then '7 rows' reaches back more than a week.
i.rows_range_none: Every store sold on every day, so 7 rows and 7 days gave identical results. They differ as soon as a day is missing.
i.explain: A shuffle (Exchange) moves rows between workers so equal keys meet. sum/avg need {a}; countDistinct needs {b} because Spark must first make (store, month, product) unique and then count. More shuffles usually means more time.
save.sizes: Size on disk: CSV {csv} MB, Parquet {pq} MB
i.prune: PartitionFilters in the plan means Spark opens only the month=3 folder and skips the other {others} {folder_word} (partition pruning).
i.prune_no_month: There is no month=3 folder in this data, so the filter month = 3 finds no files to read (only {folders} {exist}).
i.prune_missing: No PartitionFilters found in the plan; the whole dataset would be scanned.
i.size: Parquet stores columns compressed, about {ratio}x smaller than CSV here, and lets Spark read only the columns it needs.
i.size_larger: Parquet is about {ratio}x larger than CSV here: with so little data, the file and metadata overhead of {n} month {folder_word} outweighs the compression gain. The gap reverses as the data grows.
bench.table: Timings in seconds (local[*], median of the timed runs after one warm-up):
i.bench: Rows grew {rows_x}x but total time only grew {time_x}x: fixed costs (starting the JVM, scheduling tasks) dominate small data.
i.bench_small: Honest note: for a few million rows on one computer, pandas, Polars or DuckDB are often faster and simpler. Spark pays off when data or compute outgrows one machine. Your timings will differ from README numbers.

help.cmd.timezone: Extra: see how the session time zone moves month totals (UTC vs Asia/Seoul)
tz.title: [extra] Time zone trap
tz.what: Reads the data once under UTC, then recomputes the January 2025 total of one store after switching spark.sql.session.timeZone.
tz.table: {month} total of store {store} from the same stored timestamps (filtered by year-month):
i.tz: The January 2025 total changed by {diff} although no row changed: the {rows} rows from 15:00-24:00 UTC on Jan 31 ({amount}) are already February 1 in Seoul, which is 9 hours ahead. The month depends on the session time zone.
i.tz_year: Second trap: filter on the month number alone (F.month(ts) == 1) and Seoul gives {total}, because the Dec 31 15:00-24:00 UTC sales ({amount}) become January 1, 2026 and join 'month 1'. Group by year and month together.
i.tz_csv: Why a CSV hides this: its timestamps have no offset, so writing and reading in the same zone gives the same months. The trap shows when stored instants are read under another zone, as here.
notice.regenerate: Saved data has {saved_rows} rows (seed {saved_seed}) but this command asked for {rows} rows (seed {seed}), so the data is regenerated. Pass --rows {saved_rows} --seed {saved_seed} to keep and reuse the existing data.
